problem_statement: Who marks a handoff complete — the worker-loop that spawned the child runtime, or the child runtime itself after it finishes?

chosen.decision_text: Worker-loop must call completeHandoff itself on success, not delegate to the child runtime.
chosen.rationale: Worker-loop is the only process with a guaranteed gad CLI path. Codex sandbox policy blocks outbound CLI calls from inside child execution. Delegating completion to the child means any sandboxed child produces orphaned claimed-state handoffs permanently. Incident: 66 of 264 closed handoffs had completed_at:null.
evidence_refs: incident: 66 of 264 closed handoffs had completed_at:null

considered_alternatives.description: Let the child runtime (codex) call gad handoffs complete itself at the end of its execution, since it can also access the gad binary in many environments.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: Codex sandbox policy blocks child-side gad CLI calls in the common case. The child may succeed at the task but fail to mark completion, leaving the handoff in claimed-but-incomplete state indefinitely. Conditional reliability is worse than consistent worker-side completion.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: trust-the-child-to-clean-up: delegating lifecycle management to a process whose execution environment is less controlled than the parent. The parent always knows more about whether the child is alive or dead — it owns completion semantics.

considered_alternatives.description: Add a sweeper daemon as the primary mechanism that periodically scans for claimed-but-incomplete handoffs and closes them.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: Reactive not preventive. A sweeper cannot distinguish 'child is still working' from 'child died silently without completing'. It also adds a second failure mode (sweeper dying silently). Worker-side completion eliminates the orphan category; the sweeper only reduces it.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: reactive-not-preventive: treating orphan accumulation as a normal condition to be periodically cleaned rather than an invariant to be prevented at write time.

problem_statement: How do we stop Kael dual-generate and the SLM health probe from silently doubling token spend per user action?

chosen.decision_text: Disable Kael dual-generate via VITE_KAEL_DUAL_GENERATE=0 env flag; all features that multiply token spend per user action must be opt-in via explicit env flag, never default-on.
chosen.rationale: Env flag is a one-deploy fix during an active incident. The architectural rule (opt-in for multiplicative spend) is durable and generalizes to all future premium features. Health probes must never silently fall back to paid endpoints regardless of frequency.

considered_alternatives.description: Add a daily per-model token cap that cuts off dual-generate after N tokens are spent that day.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: Scope creep during an active incident. A cap requires state tracking, threshold definitions, cap-exceeded UX, and counter logic testing. None of that existed. An env flag is a one-line change. The cap can be implemented as follow-up when not under fire.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: clever-when-simple-is-right: reaching for a metered solution under incident pressure when a flag resolves the immediate bleed. Caps implemented under fire tend to have off-by-one edge cases.

considered_alternatives.description: Rate-limit the SLM health probe to once per 10 minutes instead of every 60 seconds to reduce the bleed.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: The health probe falling back to claude-sonnet is architecturally wrong regardless of frequency. Rate-limiting reduces the symptom but the behavior needs to be eliminated, not throttled.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: rate-limit-as-band-aid: reducing the frequency of an incorrect behavior rather than eliminating it. The correct fix is removal of the paid fallback path.

problem_statement: How do we prevent retry-rotation loops from draining token budgets when a premium API runtime is parked or degraded for a sustained period?

chosen.decision_text: All retry-rotation against premium APIs requires three independent guards: hard ceiling on spawns per work-unit (MAX_INNER_ROTATIONS=3), parked-runtime check before every spawn including mid-rotation, and every retry recorded in unclaim_history so per-handoff filters can trip.
chosen.rationale: Three independent guards mean any one guard miss is caught by the remaining two. Defense in depth is correct here because the cost of a single guard failure is catastrophic: the incident burned ~37M tokens because the loop had NONE of the three guards and ran unbounded against a parked runtime.

considered_alternatives.description: Add only the MAX_INNER_ROTATIONS ceiling as the single guard.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: A ceiling alone allows rotation to run MAX_INNER_ROTATIONS times against a parked runtime that will never succeed, burning tokens deterministically up to the ceiling value. The ceiling must pair with an early-exit condition (parked-check) or the savings are bounded, not eliminated.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: single-guard-single-failure: one guard has one failure mode; under the parked condition the ceiling drains tokens predictably to the ceiling value. Defense in depth exists precisely for known failure modes.

considered_alternatives.description: Remove rotation entirely and fail fast on any premium API error, treating every error as terminal for that work-unit.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: Rotation is load-bearing for multi-account setups where one account hits a rate limit but others are available. Removing it permanently degrades throughput on teams with multiple credentials. The problem was unguarded rotation, not rotation itself.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: remove-the-feature-not-the-bug: conflating a buggy implementation with a wrong abstraction. The correct surgical fix adds guards; removal trades one failure mode (token drain) for another (throughput collapse on multi-account setups).

problem_statement: How do we ensure handoff claim records are durable and agent identity is reliably traceable so claimed-but-abandoned claims can be reclaimed without orphaning work?

chosen.decision_text: Handoff claim records must carry durable agent identity (agent_id, runtime, worker_id, session_id, parent_agent_id) and a claim_lease_until field, paired with an orphan-reclaim sweeper that releases claims whose claimer is provably absent from the presence registry.
chosen.rationale: Durable identity lets the sweeper distinguish 'still working' from 'provably dead'. The lease field adds a hard deadline: if the claimer doesn't renew the lease, the sweeper reclaims. Invariant: claimed_count must not exceed live_workers + live_external_agents. Incident violated this 6:1 (55 claimed, 9 workers).

considered_alternatives.description: Increase the worker count to match or exceed the claimed count so the invariant is restored by adding capacity.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: This treats the symptom (claimed > active) by adding active workers rather than by fixing the claim lifecycle. Adding workers on top of a broken claim protocol produces a new generation of claims with the same orphan-producing properties.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: add-capacity-to-mask-breakage: restoring an invariant by scaling the denominator rather than by fixing the numerator. The invariant is a correctness property, not a capacity property.

considered_alternatives.description: Periodically wipe all stale claims via a manual operator command rather than an automated sweeper.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: Manual intervention is not a protocol. It requires the operator to notice the violation, run the command, and know the safe reclaim window. An automated sweeper with presence-registry integration provides the same result without operator attention and fires faster when agents die silently.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: manual-as-protocol: treating an operator action as a substitute for an automated invariant. Manual actions are not reliably triggered at the right time and leave a window where other agents try to pick up work that is already claimed.

problem_statement: Should an agent file a handoff to a parked or rate-limited runtime when that runtime will not be available for hours or days?

chosen.decision_text: Never file handoffs to parked/unavailable runtimes. Pre-flight check .planning/team/runtime-cooldown.json before every gad handoffs create. If target cooldown > 1 hour or most accounts are parked, reroute to an available runtime or keep the work in claude-code main thread via subagent.
chosen.rationale: A handoff to a parked runtime is a work unit that will sit unclaimed for hours. The queue grows, claimed counts drift, and the operator cannot see real progress. The mandatory pre-flight makes the routing decision at dispatch time when the information is current, not at claim time when the damage is done. Codex and OpenRouter-free-tier are routinely parked — never default-route there.
evidence_refs: corrected: 20+ times operator noted 'stop filing things off to codex'

considered_alternatives.description: File the handoff to the preferred runtime regardless of availability, and let the dispatcher retry until the runtime becomes available.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: A retry loop on a parked runtime is unbounded. Under the token-drain conditions of GLOBAL-D-331, a retry loop against a parked runtime burned 37M tokens. Routing to an available alternative or keeping the work in main thread has zero incremental risk.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: optimistic-routing-without-availability-check: treating availability as a property the runtime handles rather than a property the dispatcher must verify before filing. The dispatcher is the last point where routing is cheap to change.

considered_alternatives.description: Add a --defer flag to gad handoffs create that queues the handoff for filing when the target runtime becomes available, rather than filing immediately.
considered_alternatives.why_rejected: A defer queue adds implementation complexity and masks the availability signal from the operator. If a runtime is unavailable, the operator should know now so they can adjust the work plan. A deferred handoff that fires 3 days later when the operator has forgotten the context is worse than just routing to an available runtime today.
considered_alternatives.conceptual_failure_mode: queue-to-hide-unavailability: routing around the problem at the tooling layer rather than surfacing the constraint to the operator at decision time. Deferred handoffs become invisible work-in-progress that resurfaces at an unpredictable time.
